Give examples of natural passive immunity.
Maternal IgG that crosses the placenta, and IgA in breast milk.
Give examples of acquired passive immunity.
Immunoglobulins and antitoxins: hepatitis B immunoglobulin, tetanus immunoglobulin and rabies immunoglobulin.
Name the live attenuated vaccines of the EPI.
BCG, oral polio vaccine, measles (MR) vaccine and rotavirus vaccine (and yellow fever vaccine).
No. The whole-cell pertussis vaccine is killed. This is the classic "all are live EXCEPT" answer.
What type of vaccine is the hepatitis B vaccine?
A recombinant subunit vaccine (hepatitis B surface antigen, HBsAg).
Why are the Hib and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines joined to a protein?
Conjugation makes them work in children under 2 years and gives immune memory, through a T-cell response.
Which vaccines are given at birth in the EPI?
BCG and the birth dose of oral polio vaccine (OPV 0).
Which vaccines are given at 6 and 10 weeks?
Oral polio vaccine, pentavalent vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and rotavirus vaccine.
Which vaccines are given at 14 weeks?
The third doses of oral polio, pentavalent and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, and inactivated polio vaccine (IPV). Rotavirus vaccine is not given.
Which vaccines are given at 9 months?
The first dose of measles (MR) vaccine and meningococcal A vaccine; yellow fever vaccine in states at risk.
Which vaccine is given at 18 months?
The second dose of measles (MR) vaccine.
What does the pentavalent vaccine contain?
Diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib).
What vitamin A doses are given with the EPI?
100 000 IU at 6 months, then 200 000 IU every 6 months until 5 years of age.
By tetanus toxoid (Td) vaccination of the mother, clean delivery and clean cord care.
What are the dose and route of BCG?
0.05 ml intradermally in the left upper arm.
What are the dose and route of the measles (MR) vaccine?
0.5 ml subcutaneously in the right upper arm.
Where are the pentavalent and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines given in infants?
Intramuscularly in the anterolateral thigh: pentavalent in the left thigh and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in the right thigh.
What is the normal course after BCG vaccination?
A papule appears at 2–6 weeks, becomes a small ulcer, and heals as a scar by 3 months.
What are the complications of BCG?
Axillary lymphadenitis and abscess; disseminated BCG infection in immunodeficiency.
Which vaccine causes febrile seizures and persistent crying?
What is the rare serious complication of rotavirus vaccine?
What is the normal reaction 7–12 days after measles vaccination?
Which polio vaccine gives herd immunity and gut immunity?
Oral polio vaccine, because the vaccine virus is shed in the stool.
What is the rare complication of oral polio vaccine?
How is anaphylaxis after a vaccine treated?
Adrenaline 1:1000, 0.01 mg/kg intramuscularly, to a maximum of 0.5 ml.
What is a contraindication to all vaccines?
Anaphylaxis to a previous dose or to a component of the vaccine.
What are the contraindications to live vaccines?
Severe immunodeficiency, chemotherapy, high-dose steroids and pregnancy.
What is the absolute contraindication to pertussis vaccine?
Encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose, or a progressive neurological disease.
What is the contraindication to BCG?
Symptomatic HIV infection or a known immunodeficiency.
What are the contraindications to rotavirus vaccine?
Previous intussusception and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
Which of these is a contraindication to measles vaccine: a febrile child, a diabetic mother, or pregnancy?
Pregnancy, because the measles vaccine is live.
Are antibiotic treatment or mild diarrhoea contraindications to vaccination?
No. The child should be vaccinated.
Which polio vaccine is given to a household contact of an immunodeficient child?
Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) instead of oral polio vaccine.
How is a preterm baby vaccinated?
According to the chronological age, with full doses.
What is done when vaccine doses are missed?
The series is never restarted; it is continued with intervals of 4 weeks.
How is the newborn of an HBsAg-positive mother managed?
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, then completion of the vaccine series. Breastfeeding continues.
An unvaccinated child over 6 months old is a contact of measles. What should be given?
Measles vaccine within 72 hours of the contact.

Which extra vaccines are given in sickle cell disease?
Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPV23) after 2 years, meningococcal vaccine and yearly influenza vaccine, together with penicillin prophylaxis.
What is the rabies post-exposure schedule?
Rabies vaccine intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 14, with rabies immunoglobulin for category III exposure.
Which vaccines must never be frozen?
Pentavalent, hepatitis B and pneumococcal conjugate vaccines. The shake test detects a vaccine that has been frozen.
